fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Games That Seemed to Rehearse a Pandemic", "body": "Chance says that after the COVID era began he looked back at games from 2018 and 2019 and noticed storylines built around viruses and bioweapons, pointing to a Spider-Man title with masked crowds and curfew missions and to the early plague choice in Assassin's Creed Odyssey. Jorge recalls watching his stepchild play the Spider-Man game and noticing the same details, and he adds that most people on a big project never see the whole story, so the writers sit in the hot seat. Chance cautions that synchronicity, with art imitating life and life imitating art, means not every coincidence is deliberate programming."}, {"title": "Games, Discipline, and Short-Term Rewards", "body": "Jorge, a musician who has taught for nearly twenty five years, credits his early gaming with teaching him responsibility and how to practice toward results down the line. He worries that younger students raised on fast, big-reward mobile games struggle with the patience that scales and lessons demand. He says online lessons during the lockdowns left kids dejected by yet another screen, and he hopes the experience pushed some of them toward sunshine and friends. Chance recalls his own childhood devotion to consoles and calls today's society a de-evolution in many ways, while granting that games offer real upsides such as storytelling."}, {"title": "The Dopamine Drip of Freemium Games", "body": "Chance argues that the Dungeons and Dragons idea of leveling up has spread into nearly every genre, leaving many modern games flavored like role-playing without its virtues, and he contrasts them with Super Mario World, where the player starts with every ability. He describes idle and free-to-play phone games as menus, daily log-in rewards and an endless unlock tree, and says he knows the makers of World of Warcraft employed psychologists to keep players hooked. He likens the currency loop to universal basic income. Jorge agrees that rewards now seem to be the goal more than beating the game, noting that many phone games have no ending."}, {"title": "Mercenary Quests and the Gig Economy", "body": "Chance contends that nearly every game trains players to see a hero as a mercenary who follows a GPS marker from quest to quest and gets paid, and he argues the gig economy grew out of the same culture, with apps judging acceptance rates and an algorithm standing in for a boss. He says this strips synchronicity and entrepreneurial spirit from younger workers. Jorge agrees that games primed people for it and mourns the arcade, where neighbors helped each other with a game and lifelong friendships began, before online play and subscriptions pulled everyone home. Chance also questions whether anyone really owns something that needs an internet connection."}, {"title": "Simulacra, Positives, and Symbolic Literacy", "body": "Jorge raises Baudrillard through a cartoon character and argues the line between reality and the digital world is fading, as people expect the real world to behave like the screens they watch. He credits role-playing games with introducing him to occult imagery young, and Chance says he traced hidden inverted tarot imagery in Cyberpunk 2077, which he believes someone designed deliberately. On the positive side, Jorge cites scanning a room, attention to detail and spotting video fakery, Chance adds reflexes and hand-eye coordination, and Chance calls symbolic literacy a first line of psychic self-defense."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Musician and teacher Jorge Mesa joins InnerVerse for a chat about the emerging generations who have been raised on video games, and how society is changing as a result. What are the pros and cons of spending so much time in digital space? Is there a balance between escapism, personal responsibility, and freedom of imagination? How have these games been manipulated to socially engineer and colonize the human mind? We ask all these questions and more.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Baudrillard and the Hyperreal", "body": "Chance opens hour two with a Baudrillard line he reads aloud, that media presents a world more real than the reality we can experience. Jorge reads it through games, saying the real world loses value when people grow used to a vivid fake version, and that people now expect something from the world before giving anything to it. Chance replies that one can never actually leave reality, and he reads the quote as worldview colliding with daily experience, so that media matching a belief about outer space feels more real than life on the ground. Jorge adds a childhood story of horror-movie images making a dark hallway feel real."}, {"title": "The Gamers Paradox and Godlike Power", "body": "Chance coins what he calls the gamers paradox, dissimulating personal responsibility while simulating godhood, building on Baudrillard's contrast between pretending not to have what one has and feigning what one lacks. Jorge calls the pull toward godlike control a definite draw and wonders which comes first. Chance cites an article in which a heavy World of Warcraft player says the game makes him feel godlike while ordinary hitches feel disempowering, then argues that even a powerful character follows rules written by a programmer, a point Jorge endorses. Chance also describes dying repeatedly in the game Ghostrunner and notes that death in a game is not really death."}, {"title": "Incarnation, Dreams, and Pop Gnosticism", "body": "Chance asks whether an incarnation is a soul playing a character, mentioning that some physicists, as he has heard, suggest we simply wake in a version of reality where we did not die, like a save point, though he does not claim they are right. Jorge describes vivid deja vu dreams that he likens to a side quest and says he cannot prove them. Chance then sketches pop culture Gnosticism, with a fallen demiurge and trapped sparks of the divine, argues games echo it through architect and arch-villain figures, and suggests the belief becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. He also proposes that the body is the controller."}, {"title": "Simulation Theory as Inverted Gnosticism", "body": "Chance's theory is that simulation theory is the scientific materialist version of Gnosticism, another way to shift personal responsibility onto a dark programmer, and he calls it a dark worldview. His rebuttal is that even a player absorbed in an artificial creation never leaves reality. He argues Assassin's Creed seeds Gnostic lore in its Easter eggs, which he thinks reflects what the writers believe more than malice, and that Western baseline values make swapping a devil for a programmer easy. Jorge, for his part, observes that even a dream state is still a functioning reality, then recalls the Matrix rule that dying inside means dying outside."}, {"title": "Screens, Second Jobs, and Hope", "body": "Jorge argues that screens drain a person's life force and that television works as an input device that is programming people, and he says he lucked out by never becoming a slave to games. Chance compares guild raiding in World of Warcraft to a second job where only a few get the rewards, and both men are appalled by streamer culture aimed at children, which they say is on parents to monitor. Chance says crypto trading and streaming create little of real value, while Jorge closes with hope that humanity is not in immediate decline and Chance says spirit speaks through every moment."}]

fields.Plus Quotes JSON: [{"text": "People are starting to almost expect something from the world before they ever give anything to it.", "author": "Jorge Mesa", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/b6c1cc31-295a-4776-830c-de5410a896c0/JORGE-MESA.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "Capital R reality is existence. And as far as I know, existence is the only thing that exists.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "We have to be vigilant and monitoring what's going on in the world because we know better than we did when we were the age of anyone that we see playing these games.", "author": "Jorge Mesa", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/b6c1cc31-295a-4776-830c-de5410a896c0/JORGE-MESA.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "Here's the gamers paradox dissimulating personal responsibility while simulating godhood.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "The television seems to be an input device for us. And it really is programming.", "author": "Jorge Mesa", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/b6c1cc31-295a-4776-830c-de5410a896c0/JORGE-MESA.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "You change yourself and the world changes. You can't do it the other way around very easily, and usually oftentimes not at all.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "It's a shame that we have been convinced to lose as much time as possible on the screens.", "author": "Jorge Mesa", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/b6c1cc31-295a-4776-830c-de5410a896c0/JORGE-MESA.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "My theory on simulation theory is that it's the materialist, like the reductionist scientific materialist version of Gnosticism.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "Humanity isn't in some state of immediate decline and some readily available apocalypse that will totally wipe out humanity. We're doing pretty good, I'd say.", "author": "Jorge Mesa", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/b6c1cc31-295a-4776-830c-de5410a896c0/JORGE-MESA.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "Everything that we experience is for a reason, and there's always spirit speaking to us through every moment.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}]
fields.Quotes JSON: [{"text": "I look at today's society in a lot of ways as a de-evolution from times gone by.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "The rewards do seem to be the goal more than you even beating the game.", "author": "Jorge Mesa", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/b6c1cc31-295a-4776-830c-de5410a896c0/JORGE-MESA.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "We are going to have a realistic chat about how social engineering has been achieved through these games and how it's worked its magic for good and bad on our generation.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "The distinction between reality and the digital world is really going away very quickly, where people are absolutely expecting the real world to behave like the digital world that they're presented with.", "author": "Jorge Mesa", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/b6c1cc31-295a-4776-830c-de5410a896c0/JORGE-MESA.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "The gig economy thing, I think, is spun straight out of game culture and is a very negative manifestation of how things are going.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "You meet people through your community. You experience the synchronicity of showing up to an arcade, and then that person you saw two weeks ago is there again.", "author": "Jorge Mesa", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/b6c1cc31-295a-4776-830c-de5410a896c0/JORGE-MESA.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "I say it all the time, but symbolic literacy is psychic self-defense.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "What is easier to manipulate than a computer? The damn thing does exactly what you tell it to every single time and without fail.", "author": "Jorge Mesa", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/b6c1cc31-295a-4776-830c-de5410a896c0/JORGE-MESA.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}]
